extraction_notes.note: Duplicate \label keys: thm:BLvsGS (Theorems 1 and 2), thm:GNNS (Theorems 4 and 5), thm:sparse (Theorem 9 and Corollary 1), eq:nonlinear_approx ((4) and (8)); refs resolve to the first. The proof of Theorem 11 cites thm:sparse but uses Corollary 1's 2T bound, so a CP1->PP12 edge was added by hand.
Section 5.3.1 repeats the nonlinear-approximation paragraph and equation (8) verbatim from (4), and repeats the NMSE formula unnumbered; only the first copies are nodes.

Labelled but unnumbered displays (eq:PLS, eq:C, eq:Delta, eq:trend_filtering) appear as equation facts; following the rule that unnumbered displays are not nodes, they stay inside their containing nodes. The two \eqref{eq:PLS} occur in experiment prose that is not a node.
One sentence (joined by semicolons) introduces V_L, V_P and V_W; kept as one definition because splitting would break the whole-sentence rule.
These prose nodes start right after a \mypar{...} paragraph heading macro, which the boundary check reports as mid-sentence; the statements start at the first word of the paragraph text.
Theorem 12 concludes P(Reject) <= delta under H_1 (presumably meant >= 1-delta), and Theorem 2's condition uses lambda_k with lowercase k; copied verbatim.
The classical time-frequency uncertainty principle is stated only in words with citations; kept as an external theorem (generalized by Theorem 5) rather than as an applied citation.
The three relaxed partition methods adapt cited techniques (spectral clustering, balance cut of a spanning tree, k-means); given origin paper as the paper's own relaxations of problem (7).

The case studies (coauthor network, SIS epidemics, SO2 change detection), dataset descriptions, figures and the author table are not extracted; only headline experimental findings are numerical claims.
Theorem 6 says it was 'shown in the previous section'; the prose paragraph checking the MRA requirements, which comes before the theorem, is taken as its proof.

nodes.name: Weighted graph $\mathcal{G}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}, \mathrm{W})$  be a directed, irregular and weighted graph, where $\mathcal{V} = \{v_i \}_{i=1}^N$ is the set of nodes, $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of weighted edges, and $\mathrm{W} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ is the weighted adjacency matrix, whose element $\mathrm{W}_{i,j}$ measures the underlying relation between the $i$th and the $j$th nodes.
nodes.genus: a directed, irregular and weighted graph
nodes.statement_short: Graph with node set, weighted edge set and weighted adjacency matrix W.

nodes.name: Degree vector
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{d} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N$ be a degree vector, where $d_i = \sum_j \mathrm{W}_{i,j}$.

nodes.name: Graph signal
nodes.statement:
Given a fixed ordering of nodes, we assign a signal coefficient to each node; a~\emph{graph signal} is then defined as a vector,
$$
	\mathbf{x} = [x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_N]^T \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N,
$$
with $x_n$ the signal coefficient corresponding to the node $v_n$.

nodes.name: Graph shift operator
nodes.statement: We use the graph shift operator $\mathrm{A} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ as a graph representation, which is an elementary filtering operation that replaces a signal coefficient at a node with a weighted linear combination of coefficients at its neighboring nodes.

nodes.name: Normalized adjacency and transition matrix
nodes.statement: Some common choices of a graph shift are weighted adjacency matrix $\mathrm{W}$, normalized adjacency matrix $\mathrm{W}_{\rm norm} = {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-\frac{1}{2}} \mathrm{W} {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, and transition matrix $\mathrm{P} = {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-1} \mathrm{W}$~\cite{ChenSMK:13}.
nodes.statement_short: Common graph shifts: W, normalized adjacency W_norm = D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}, and transition matrix P = D^{-1} W.

nodes.name: Graph Laplacian matrix
nodes.statement: The second one is based on the spectral graph theory~\cite{Chung:96}, where the graph Laplacian matrix $\mathrm{L} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ is used  as a graph representation, which is a second-order difference operator on graphs.
nodes.genus: a second-order difference operator on graphs

nodes.name: Unnormalized, normalized and transition Laplacians
nodes.statement: Some common choices of a graph Laplacian matrix are the unnormalized Laplacian  ${\rm diag}(\mathbf{d}) - \mathrm{W}$, the normalized Laplacian  $\mathrm{I} - {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-\frac{1}{2}} \mathrm{W} {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, and the transition Laplacian $\mathrm{I} - {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-1} \mathrm{W} $.
nodes.statement_short: Common Laplacians: diag(d)-W, I - D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}, and I - D^{-1} W.

nodes.name: Graph structure matrix $\mathrm{R}$
nodes.statement: We use $\mathrm{R} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ to represent a graph structure matrix, which can be either a graph shift or a graph Laplacian matrix.
differentia: either a graph shift or a graph Laplacian matrix

nodes.name: Graph Fourier basis
Graph Fourier transform
nodes.statement:
The graph Fourier transform \rm{of $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$} is 
$
	\widehat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathrm{U} \mathbf{x},
$
where $\mathrm{U} = \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ is called the graph Fourier transform matrix.

nodes.name: Inverse graph Fourier transform
nodes.statement:
The~\textit{inverse graph Fourier transform} is
$
	\mathbf{x} =  \mathrm{V}  \widehat{\mathbf{x}}.
$

nodes.name: Variation with respect to a graph shift
nodes.statement_short: Shift-based variation: squared distance between x and its normalized shift A x / |lambda_max(A)|.

nodes.name: Eigenvalue order gives variation order (graph shift)
nodes.statement: We can show that when the eigenvalues of the graph shift $\mathrm{A} $ are sorted in a nonincreasing order $\lambda^{(\mathrm{A})}_1 \geq \lambda^{(\mathrm{A})}_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda^{(\mathrm{A})}_N$, the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follow a nondecreasing order $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{A}}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{A})}_1) \leq \mathrm{S}_{(\mathrm{A})}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{A})}_2) \leq \ldots \leq \mathrm{S}_{(\mathrm{A})}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{A})}_N)$.
assumptions: when the eigenvalues of the graph shift $\mathrm{A} $ are sorted in a nonincreasing order
conclusions: the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follow a nondecreasing order
nodes.statement_short: Eigenvectors of A sorted by decreasing eigenvalue have nondecreasing shift-variation.

nodes.name: Variation with respect to the graph Laplacian
nodes.statement:
When the graph representation matrix is the graph Laplacian matrix, the variation of a graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ is defined as,
 \begin{equation*} 	\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{L}} (\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i,j=1}^N \mathrm{A}_{i,j}(x_i-x_j)^2 = \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Eigenvalue order gives variation order (Laplacian)
nodes.statement: Similarly, we can show that when the eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian $\mathrm{L}$ are sorted in a nondecreasing order $\lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_1 \leq \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_2 \leq \ldots \leq \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_N$, the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follows a nondecreasing order $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{L}}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_1) \leq \mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{L}}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_2) \leq \ldots \leq \mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{L}}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_N)$.
assumptions: when the eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian $\mathrm{L}$ are sorted in a nondecreasing order
conclusions: the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follows a nondecreasing order
nodes.statement_short: Laplacian eigenvectors sorted by increasing eigenvalue have nondecreasing quadratic-form variation.

nodes.name: Low- and high-frequency components
nodes.statement: The variations of graph Fourier basis vectors thus allow us to provide the ordering:  the Fourier basis vectors with small variations are considered as \textit{low-frequency} components while the vectors with large variations are considered as \textit{high-frequency} components~\cite{SandryhailaM:131}.

nodes.name: Graph Fourier bases ordered from low to high frequency
nodes.statement: In the following discussion, we assume all graph Fourier bases are ordered from low frequencies to high frequencies.

nodes.name: Descriptive graph signal model
nodes.statement:
For the descriptive approach, we describe the properties of a graph signal by bounding the output of some operator. Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a graph signal, $f(\cdot)$ be a function operating on $\mathbf{x}$, we define a class of graph signals by restricting
\begin{equation} f(\mathbf{x})  \leq C,
\end{equation}
where $C$ is some constant.
nodes.statement_short: A signal class defined by bounding an operator output, f(x) <= C.

nodes.name: Descriptive model constraint
nodes.statement: f(\mathbf{x}) \leq C,
nodes.label: eq:descriptive

nodes.name: Generative graph signal model
nodes.statement_short: A signal class defined as x = D a for a graph dictionary D.

nodes.name: Passive graph dictionary design
Active graph dictionary design
Frame bounds of a graph dictionary
Sparse representation property
Uncertainty principle property of a dictionary
nodes.statement_short: For two sub-dictionaries, the sparsities of epsilon-approximations in each sum to at least C.

nodes.name: Sparse coding problem
nodes.statement:
We consider approximating a graph signal by using a linear combination of a few atoms from $\mathrm{D}$ and solving the following sparse coding problem,
\begin{eqnarray} \mathbf{x}^*, \mathbf{a}^*=  &  \arg \min_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{a}} & d(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x} ),
   \\
   \nonumber
   & {\rm subject~to:~} & \mathbf{x}' = \mathrm{D} \mathbf{a}, 
   \\
   \nonumber
   && \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K.
\end{eqnarray}
where $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ is some evaluation metric.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate a graph signal by at most K atoms of dictionary D, minimizing a metric d.

nodes.name: Sparse coding problem (2)
nodes.statement: \mathbf{x}^*, \mathbf{a}^*= & \arg \min_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{a}} & d(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x} ), \\ \nonumber & {\rm subject~to:~} & \mathbf{x}' = \mathrm{D} \mathbf{a}, \\ \nonumber && \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K.
nodes.label: eq:sparse_coding

nodes.name: Sampling operator
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathrm{F} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ be a sampling pattern matrix, which is constrained by a given application and the sampling operator is 
\begin{equation} \Psi = \mathrm{C} \mathrm{F} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{M \times N},
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{C} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{M \times N}$ selects rows from $\mathrm{F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sampling operator Psi = C F: a row selection C of a sampling pattern matrix F.

nodes.name: Sampling operator (3)
nodes.statement: \Psi = \mathrm{C} \mathrm{F} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{M \times N},
nodes.label: eq:Psi

nodes.name: Sampling strategies: uniform, experimentally designed, active
nodes.statement: There are three sampling strategies: (1) uniform sampling when designing $\mathrm{C}$, , where row indices are chosen from from $\{0, 1, \cdots, N-1\}$ independently and uniformly; and~\emph{experimentally design sampling}, where row indices can be chosen beforehand; and~\emph{active sampling}, where we will use feedback as samples are sequentially collected to decide the next row to be sampled.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform sampling (random rows), experimentally designed sampling (rows chosen beforehand) and active sampling (sequential, feedback-driven).

nodes.name: Subsampling and compressed sampling operators
nodes.statement: The sampling pattern matrix $\mathrm{F}$ constraints the following sampling patterns: when $\mathrm{F}$ is an identity matrix, $\Psi$ is a subsampling operator; when $\mathrm{F}$ is a Gaussian random matrix,  $\Psi$ is a compressed sampling operator.

nodes.name: Sampling phase (noisy samples)
nodes.statement:
In the sampling phase, we take
samples with the sampling operator $\Psi$,
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{x}_{\Psi} = \Psi \mathbf{y} = \Psi ( \mathbf{x}  + \epsilon),
\end{equation*}
 is a vector of samples and $\epsilon$ is
noise with zero mean and $\sigma^2$ as variance.

nodes.name: Recovery operator
nodes.statement:
In the recovery phase, we
reconstruct the graph signal by using a recovery operator $\Phi$, 
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{x}' = \Phi \mathbf{x}_{\Psi},
\end{equation*}
where $\mathbf{x}'$ recovers $\mathbf{x}$ either
exactly or approximately.

nodes.name: Prototype sampling and recovery design problem
nodes.statement:
The prototype of designing sampling and recovery strategies is
\begin{eqnarray*}
\Psi^*(\mathrm{D}), \Phi^*(\mathrm{D}) = \min_{\Psi, \Phi} \max_{\mathbf{a}} && d(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}),
\\
 {\rm subject~to} && \mathbf{x}' = \Phi \Psi (\mathbf{x} + \epsilon),
\\
&& \mathbf{x} = \mathrm{D} \mathbf{a},
\end{eqnarray*}
where $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ is some evaluation metric.
nodes.statement_short: Minimax design of sampling Psi and recovery Phi over signals x = D a.

nodes.name: Pairwise Lipschitz smooth graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ with unit norm is~\emph{pairwise Lipschitz smooth} with parameter $C$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} | x_i - x_j | \ \leq \ C \ d(v_i, v_j),~{\rm for~all~} i,j = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1, \end{equation*} with $d(v_i, v_j)$ the distance between the $i$th and the $j$th nodes.
nodes.genus: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ with unit norm
nodes.label: df:pairwise_Lip

nodes.name: Total Lipschitz smooth graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ with unit norm is~\emph{total Lipschitz smooth} with parameter $C$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{E}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} ( x_i - x_j )^2 \ \leq \ C. \end{equation*}
nodes.genus: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ with unit norm
nodes.label: df:global_Lip

nodes.name: Local normalized neighboring smooth graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ with unit norm is~\emph{local normalized neighboring smooth } with parameter $C$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \sum_i \left( x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j: (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} } \sum_{j: (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j \right)^2 \ \leq \ C. \end{equation*}
nodes.genus: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ with unit norm
nodes.statement_short: Sum over nodes of squared deviation from the local weighted average of neighbors is at most C.
nodes.label: df:local_neighboring_smooth

nodes.name: Global normalized neighboring smooth graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ with unit norm is~\emph{global normalized neighboring smooth} with parameter $C$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \sum_i \left( x_i - \frac{1}{ |\lambda_{\max}(\mathrm{W})| } \sum_{j: (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j \right)^2 \ \leq \ C. \end{equation*}
nodes.genus: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ with unit norm
nodes.statement_short: Sum of squared deviations from the neighbor sum normalized by |lambda_max(W)| is at most C.
nodes.label: df:global_neighboring_smooth

nodes.name: Polynomial graph signal / graph polynomial dictionary
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ is polynomial with degree $K$ when \begin{equation*} \mathbf{x} \ = \ \mathrm{D}_{\rm poly(K)} \mathbf{a} \ = \ \begin{bmatrix} {\bf 1} & \mathrm{D}^{(1)} & \mathrm{D}^{(2)} & \ldots & \mathrm{D}^{(K)} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{a} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N, \end{equation*} where $\mathbf{a} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{KN+1}$ and $\mathrm{D}_{\rm poly(K)} $ is a graph polynomial dictionary with $\mathrm{D}^{(k)}_{i,j} = d^k(v_i, v_j)$. Denote this class by $\mathrm{PL}(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: x = D_poly(K) a with atoms d^k(v_i, v_j) from every node as origin; class PL(K).
nodes.label: df:polynomial_sig

nodes.name: Graph polynomial dictionary represents the pairwise Lipschiz smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf Graph polynomial dictionary represents the pairwise Lipschiz smooth signals}) $\mathrm{PL}(1)$ is a subset of the pairwise Lipschitz smooth with some parameter $C$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{PL}(1)$ is a subset of the pairwise Lipschitz smooth with some parameter $C$.
nodes.label: thm:BLvsGS

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{PL}(1)$, that is, $$ \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} {\bf 1} & \mathrm{D}^{(1)} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{a}, $$ Then, we write the pairwise Lipschitz smooth criterion as \begin{eqnarray*} |x_i - x_j| & = & | \sum_{k} \left( d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) \right) a_k | \\ & \leq & \sum_{k} | d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) | |a_k | \\ \\ & \leq & \sum_{k} |a_k | | d(v_i, v_j) | \ = \ \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_1 | d(v_i, v_j) |. \end{eqnarray*} The parameter $C = \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_1$, which corresponds to the energy of the original graph signal.
nodes.statement_short: Expand x in the distance atoms and bound |x_i - x_j| via the triangle inequality, giving C = ||a||_1.

nodes.name: Bandlimited graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ is bandlimited with respect to a graph Fourier basis $\mathrm{V}$ with bandwidth $K$ when \begin{equation*} \mathbf{x} = \mathrm{V}_{(K)} \mathbf{a}, \end{equation*} where $\mathbf{a} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{K}$ and $\mathrm{V}_{(K)}$ is a submatrix containing the first $K$ columns of $\mathrm{V}$. Denote this class by $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}}(K)$~\cite{ChenVSK:15}.

nodes.name: Notation $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}$, $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}$, $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}$
nodes.statement: When $\mathrm{V}$ is the eigenvector matrix of the unnormalized graph Laplacian matrix, we denote it as $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}$ and can show that signals in $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}}(K)$ are total Lipschitz smooth; when $\mathrm{V}$ is the eigenvector matrix of the transition matrix, we denote it as $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}$ and can show that signals in $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}}(K)$ are local normalized neighboring smooth; when $\mathrm{V}$ is the eigenvector matrix of the weighted adjacency matrix, we denote it as $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}$ and can show that signals in $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}}(K)$ are global normalized neighboring smooth.
nodes.statement_short: V_L, V_P, V_W denote eigenvector matrices of the unnormalized Laplacian, transition matrix and adjacency matrix.

nodes.name: The graph Fourier basis of the graph Laplacian represents the total Lipschiz smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf The graph Fourier basis of the graph Laplacian represents the total Lipschiz smooth signals}) For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$, $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}}(K)$ is a subset of the total Lipschitz smooth with parameter $C$, when $C \geq \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_k$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}}(K)$ is a subset of the total Lipschitz smooth with parameter $C$
nodes.label: thm:BLvsGS

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a graph signal with bandwidth $K$, that is, $$ \mathbf{x} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_k, $$ Then, we write the total Lipschitz smooth criterion as \begin{eqnarray*} && \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{E}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} ( x_i - x_j )^2 \ = \ \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x} \\ & = & (\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_k)^T (\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \widehat{x}_k \lambda_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_k) \ = \ \sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_k \widehat{x}_k^2 \\ & \leq & \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_K \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k^2 \ = \ \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_K. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Write x^T L x in the Laplacian eigenbasis and bound by the K-th eigenvalue.

nodes.name: The graph Fourier basis of the transition matrix represents the local normalized neighboring smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf The graph Fourier basis of the transition matrix represents the local normalized neighboring smooth signals}) For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$, $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}}(K)$ is a subset of the local normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$, when $C \geq (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K})^2$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}}(K)$ is a subset of the local normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$
nodes.label: thm:LNNS

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a graph signal with bandwidth $K$, that is, $$ \mathbf{x} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k, $$ Then, we write the local normalized neighboring smooth criterion as \begin{eqnarray*} && \left| x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} } \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j \right| \\ &= & \left| \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k \right)_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{P}_{i,j} \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k \right)_j \right| \\ & = & \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \left( (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{P}_{i,j} (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_j \right) \right| \\ & = & \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k (1 - \lambda_k) (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_i \right| \\ & \leq & (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K}) \left| \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \widehat{x}_k (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_i \right| \ = \ (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K}) |x_i|. \end{eqnarray*} The last equality follows from the fact that $\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k$ and $\lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_k$ are eigenvectors and eigenvalues of $\mathrm{P}$. \begin{eqnarray*} && \sum_i \left( x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i }} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i } \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j \right)^2 \\ & = & \sum_{i=1}^{N} |x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} } \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j |^2 \\ & \leq & \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K} )^2 |x_i|^2 \ = \ (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K})^2 . \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Use that v_k^(P) are eigenvectors of P to bound each node's deviation by (1 - lambda_K) |x_i|, then sum squares.

nodes.name: The graph Fourier basis of the adjacency matrix represents the global normalized neighboring smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf The graph Fourier basis of the adjacency matrix represents the global normalized neighboring smooth signals}) For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$, $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}}(K)$ is a subset of the global normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$, when $C \geq (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{W})}_{K} / |\lambda_{\max}{(\mathrm{W})}| )^2$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}}(K)$ is a subset of the global normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$
nodes.label: thm:GNNS

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to Theorem~\ref{thm:LNNS}.
nodes.statement_short: Analogous to the proof of Theorem 3, with the adjacency matrix in place of the transition matrix.

nodes.name: Frame bounds of smooth-signal dictionaries
nodes.statement: Graph polynomial dictionary is highly redundant and the frame bound is loose. When the graph is undirected, the adjacency matrix is symmetric, then $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}$ are orthonormal. It is hard to draw any meaningful conclusion when the graph is directed; we leave it for the future work.

nodes.name: Sparse representations of smooth-signal dictionaries
nodes.statement: Graph polynomial dictionary provides sparse representations for polynomial graph signals. On the other hand, the graph Fourier bases provide sparse representations for the bandlimited graph signals. For approximately bandlimited graph signals, there are some residuals coming from the high-frequency components.

nodes.name: Classical time-frequency uncertainty principle
nodes.statement: In classical signal processing, it is well known that signals cannot localize in both time and frequency domains at the same time~\cite{VetterliKG:12, DonohoS:89}.
conclusions: signals cannot localize in both time and frequency domains at the same time

nodes.name: $\epsilon$-vertex concentrated graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ is~\emph{$\epsilon$-vertex concentrated} on a graph vertex set $\Gamma$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon, \end{equation*} where $\mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ is a diagonal matrix, with $(\mathrm{I}_{\Gamma})_{i,i} = 1$ when $i \in \Gamma$ and $0$, otherwise.
nodes.label: df:concentrate_v

nodes.name: $\epsilon$-spectrum concentrated graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ is~\emph{$\epsilon$-spectrum concentrated} on a graph spectrum band $\Omega$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon, \end{equation*} where $ \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times |\Omega|}$ is a submatrix of $\mathrm{V}$ with columns selected by $\Omega$ and $ \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{|\Omega| \times N}$ is a submatrix of $\mathrm{V}$ with rows selected by $\Omega$.
nodes.label: df:concentrate_s

nodes.name: Uncertainty principle of the graph vertex and spectrum domains
nodes.statement: ({\bf Uncertainty principle of the graph vertex and spectrum domains}) Let a unit norm signal $\mathbf{x}$ supported on an undirected graph be $\epsilon_{\Gamma}$-vertex concentrated and $\epsilon_{\Omega}$-spectrum concentrated at the same time. Then, \begin{equation*} |\Gamma| \cdot |\Omega| \geq \frac{(1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ))^2 }{ \left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 }. \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let a unit norm signal $\mathbf{x}$ supported on an undirected graph be $\epsilon_{\Gamma}$-vertex concentrated and $\epsilon_{\Omega}$-spectrum concentrated at the same time.
conclusions: |\Gamma| \cdot |\Omega| \geq \frac{(1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ))^2 }{ \left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 }.
nodes.statement_short: A signal concentrated on vertex set Gamma and spectral band Omega has |Gamma||Omega| >= (1-eps)^2 / ||U_Omega||_inf^2.
nodes.label: thm:GNNS

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5
nodes.statement: We first show $\left\| \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \right\|_2 \leq \left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty} \sqrt{ |\Gamma|\cdot |\Omega|}$. \begin{eqnarray*} && ( \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \mathbf{x} )_s \ = \ \sum_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{V}_{s,k} \left( \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \mathrm{U}_{k,i} x_i \right) \\ & = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left( \sum_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{V}_{s,k} \mathrm{U}_{k,i} \right) x_i \ = \ \sum_i q(s,i) x_i, \end{eqnarray*} where \begin{equation*} q(s,i) = \left\{ \begin{array}{rl} \sum_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{V}_{s,k} \mathrm{U}_{k,i}, & i \in \Gamma;\\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise}. \end{array} \right. \end{equation*} Let $\mathbf{y}^{(i)}$ be a graph signal with $y^{(i)}_s = q(s,i)$. Then, $( \widehat{\mathbf{y}^{(i)}} )_k = {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{U}_{k,i}$. We then have \begin{eqnarray*} && \left\| \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \right\|_{2}^2 \ \leq \ \left\| \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \right\|_{\rm HS}^2 \\ & = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{s} |q(s,i)|^2 \ = \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left\| \mathbf{y}^{(i)} \right\|_2^2 \\ & = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left\| \widehat{ \mathbf{y}^{(i)} } \right\|_2^2 \ = \ \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{k} \left( {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{U}_{k,i} \right)^2 \\ & \leq & \left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{k} {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \ = \ \left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 |\Gamma| \cdot |\Omega|. \end{eqnarray*} We then show that $\left\| \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \mathbf{x} \right\|_2 \geq 1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} )$. Based on the assumption, we have \begin{eqnarray*} && \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \mathbf{x} \right\|_2 \\ & = & \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \mathbf{x} \right\|_2 + \left\| \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \mathbf{x} \right\|_2 \\ & \leq & \epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma}. \end{eqnarray*} Since $\mathbf{x}$ has a unit norm, by the triangle inequality, we have \begin{equation*} \left\| \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \right\|_2 \geq 1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ). \end{equation*} Finally, we combine two results and obtain \begin{equation*} |\Gamma|\cdot |\Omega| \geq \frac{\left\| \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \right\|_2^2}{\left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 } \ > \ \frac{ (1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ))^2 }{ \left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Upper-bound the operator norm of V_Omega U_Omega I_Gamma by its Hilbert-Schmidt norm, lower-bound it by concentration and the triangle inequality, then combine.

nodes.name: Graph signals can localize in both vertex and spectrum domains
nodes.statement: We see that the lower bound involves with the maximum magnitude of $\mathrm{U}_{\Omega}$. In classical signal processing, $\mathrm{U}$ is the discrete Fourier transform matrix, so $\left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}  = 1/\sqrt{N}$; the lower bound is $O(N)$ and signals cannot localize in both time and frequency domain. However, for complex and irregular graphs, the energy of a graph Fourier basis vector may concentrate on a few elements, that is, $\left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty} = O(1)$, as shown in Figures~\ref{fig:geo_fourier}(a)(b)(c)(d). It is thus possible that  graph signals can be localized in both the vertex and spectrum domain.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike the DFT (||U||_inf = 1/sqrt N), graph Fourier bases can be localized, so the lower bound can be O(1).

nodes.name: Localization of a graph signal
nodes.statement: The \textit{localization} of a graph signal means that most elements in a graph signal are zeros, or have small values; only a small number of elements have large magnitudes and the corresponding nodes are clustered in one subgraph with a small diameter.

nodes.name: Inverse participation ratio (IPR)
Energy concentration ratio (ECR)
nodes.statement:
To solve this, we propose a novel measure to quantify the localization of a graph signal. We use \textit{energy concentration ratio} (ECR) to quantify the energy concentration property. The ECR is defined as 
\begin{equation*}
\rm{ECR} = \frac{S^*}{N},
\end{equation*}
where $S^*$ is the smallest $S$ that satisfies
$
\left\| \mathbf{x}_S \right\|_2^2 \geq 95\%  \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2,
$
with $\mathbf{x}_S$ the first $S$ elements with the largest magnitude in $\mathbf{x}$.
nodes.statement_short: ECR = S*/N, with S* the fewest largest-magnitude entries holding 95% of the energy.

nodes.name: Normalized geodesic distance (NGD)
nodes.statement_short: Average pairwise geodesic distance among the nodes holding 95% of the energy, divided by the graph diameter.

nodes.name: Localized graph Fourier basis
nodes.statement: Each graph Fourier basis vector is regarded as a graph signal. When most basis vectors in the graph Fourier basis are localized, that is, the corresponding ECRs and NGDs are small, we call that graph Fourier basis localized.

nodes.name: Graph Fourier bases of real networks are localized
nodes.statement: We find that a large number of graph Fourier basis vectors has small ECRs and NGDs, which indicates that graph Fourier basis vectors of various graph representation matrices are localized. Among various graph representation matrices, the graph Fourier basis vectors of graph Laplacian matrix tend to be more localized, especially in high-frequency components. In low-frequency components, the graph Fourier basis vectors of adjacency matrix are more localized.
conclusions: graph Fourier basis vectors of various graph representation matrices are localized
nodes.statement_short: On the arXiv GrQc network many Fourier basis vectors have small ECR and NGD; Laplacian vectors localize at high frequencies, adjacency vectors at low.

nodes.name: Nonlinear approximation
nodes.statement:
Let $\{ \phi_k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N \}_{k=1}^N$ and  $\{ \widehat{\phi}_k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N \}_{k=1}^N$ be a pair of biorthonormal basis and $\mathbf{x} \in  \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N $ be a signal. Here the graph Fourier transform matrix $\mathrm{U} = \{ \widehat{\phi}_k \}_{k=1}^N$ and the graph Fourier basis $\mathrm{V} = \{ \phi_k \}_{k=1}^N$. The nonlinear approximation to $\mathbf{x}$ is 
\begin{eqnarray} \mathbf{x}^* = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}_K} \left\langle {\mathbf{x}, \widehat{\phi}_k} \right\rangle \phi_k,
\end{eqnarray}
where $\mathcal{I}_K$ is the index set of the $K$ largest-magnitude expansion coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: Keep the K largest-magnitude expansion coefficients in a biorthonormal basis pair.

nodes.name: Nonlinear approximation (4)
nodes.statement: \mathbf{x}^* = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}_K} \left\langle {\mathbf{x}, \widehat{\phi}_k} \right\rangle \phi_k,
nodes.label: eq:nonlinear_approx

nodes.name: $\ell_2$ sparse coding with the graph polynomial dictionary
nodes.statement:
Since the the graph polynomial dictionary is redundant, we solve the following sparse coding problem,
\begin{eqnarray} \mathbf{x}^* =  &  \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}} & \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{D}_{\rm poly(2)} \mathbf{a}  \right\|_2^2,
   \\
   \nonumber
   & {\rm subject~to:~} &  \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K,
\end{eqnarray}
where $\mathrm{D}_{\rm poly(2)}$ is the graph polynomial dictionary with order $2$ and $\mathbf{a}$ are expansion coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate x by at most K atoms of D_poly(2) in l2 norm.

nodes.name: Sparse coding with D_poly(2) (5)
nodes.statement: \mathbf{x}^* = & \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}} & \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{D}_{\rm poly(2)} \mathbf{a} \right\|_2^2, \\ \nonumber & {\rm subject~to:~} & \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K,
nodes.label: eq:l2_sparse_coding

nodes.name: Normalized mean square error
nodes.statement:
To make a more serious comparison, we evaluate the approximation error by using the normalized mean square error, that is,
\begin{equation} {\rm Normalized~MSE} = \frac{ \left\|  \mathbf{x}^* - \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 }{ \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 },
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{x}^*$ is the approximation signal and $\mathbf{x}$ is the original signal.

nodes.name: Normalized MSE (6)
nodes.statement: {\rm Normalized~MSE} = \frac{ \left\| \mathbf{x}^* - \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 }{ \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 },
nodes.label: eq:NMSE

nodes.name: Approximation of wind speed: V_L, D_poly(2), V_P beat V_W
nodes.statement: We see that $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $\mathrm{D}_{\rm poly(2)}$ tie $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}$; all of them are much better than $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}$.
conclusions: all of them are much better than $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}$

nodes.name: Energy of expansion coefficients concentrated on a known support
nodes.statement: In general, we assume that the energy of the expansion coefficient $\mathbf{a}$ is concentrated in a few known supports, that is, $\left\| \mathbf{a}_{\Omega} \right\|_2 \gg \left\| \mathbf{a}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_2$, where $|\Omega| \ll N $ and $\Omega$ is the known.

nodes.name: Partial least squares (PLS) recovery
nodes.statement:
We consider the partial least squares (PLS), $x^*_{\rm PLS}  \ = \  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega}  \mathbf{a}^*_{\rm PLS} $, where
\begin{eqnarray} \mathbf{a}^*_{\rm PLS}  & = & 	
	  \arg \min_{ \mathbf{a}}  \left\|  \Psi^T \mathbf{x}_{\Psi} -  \Psi^T \Psi  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \mathbf{a}_{\Omega} \right\|_2^2
	\nonumber
	\\
	& = &   \left(  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega}^T \Psi^T \Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \right)^{-1}  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \Psi^T \Psi \mathbf{y}
	\nonumber
	\\
	\nonumber
	& = & (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi ( \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \mathbf{a}_{\Omega} + \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \mathbf{a}_{\Omega^c}  + \epsilon ),
\end{eqnarray}
where $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + \epsilon$ is the noisy version of the graph signal with $\epsilon$ is noise, $(\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi = \left(  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega}^T \mathrm{S}  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \right)^{-1}  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega}^T \mathrm{S}$ and $\mathrm{S} =  \Psi^T \Psi$, which is a diagonal matrix with $\mathrm{S}_{i,i}= 1$, when the $i$th node is sampled, and 0, otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Recover a_Omega by least squares on the samples, x*_PLS = D_Omega (Psi D_Omega)^dagger Psi y.

nodes.name: PLS recovery error decomposition
conclusions: \mathbf{x}^*_{\rm PLS}  - \mathbf{x}
nodes.statement_short: PLS error = D_Omega (Psi D_Omega)^dagger Psi (D_{Omega^c} a_{Omega^c} + noise): a bias plus a noise-variance term.

nodes.name: Optimal sampling settings (a)-(f)
nodes.statement:
We aim to optimize the sampling strategy by minimizing the recovery error and there are six cases to be considered: 
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
	\item minimizing the bias in the worst case; that is,	
	$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_2,
	$$
	where $ \sigma_{\max}$ is the largest singular value;
	\item minimizing the bias in expectation; that is,	
	$$
	\min_{S}   \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi   \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_{F}^2,
	$$
	where $\left\| \cdot \right\|_F$ is the Frobenius norm;
	\item minimizing the variance from noise in the worst case; that is,	
	$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \right\|_2;
	$$
	\item minimizing the variance from noise in expectation; that is,	
	$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \right\|_F;
	$$
	\item minimizing the recovery error in worst case, that is,
$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_2	+ c \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \right\|_2,
$$
	where $c$ is related to the signal-to-noise ratio;
	\item minimizing the recovery error in expectation; that is,
$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_F + c \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \right\|_F,
$$
	where $c$ is related to the signal-to-noise ratio.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Six criteria for choosing Psi: worst-case/expected bias, noise variance, or total recovery error of PLS.

nodes.name: Optimal sampling operator
nodes.statement: We call the resulting sampling operator $\Psi$ of each setting as an~\emph{optimal sampling operator with respect to setting ($\cdot$)}.
nodes.definiendum: optimal sampling operator with respect to setting ($\cdot$)

nodes.name: Row-subset matrix approximation of a graph structure matrix
Row-sampling reconstruction bound (Boutsidis-Drineas-Magdon-Ismail)
assumptions: where $\mathrm{R}_K$ is the best rank $K$ approximation of $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{V}_{(K)}$ is the first $K$ columns of the graph Fourier transform matrix of $\mathrm{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruction error from sampled rows is at most the best rank-K error times ||(Psi V_(K))^dagger Psi||_2^2.

nodes.name: Optimal sampling operator (c) preserves graph-structure information
nodes.statement: We see that when $\mathrm{D}_{\Omega} = \mathrm{V}_{(K)}$, the rows sampled by the optimal sampling operator in (c) minimize the reconstruction error of the graph structure matrix.
conclusions: the rows sampled by the optimal sampling operator in (c) minimize the reconstruction error of the graph structure matrix

nodes.name: Greedy optimal sampling performs best
nodes.statement: Within three optimal sampling operators, the greedy search algorithm provides the best performance.
conclusions: the greedy search algorithm provides the best performance

nodes.name: Graph difference operator
nodes.statement:
Let $\Delta$ be the~\emph{graph difference
  operator} (the oriented incidence matrix of $G$), whose rows
correspond to edges~\cite{SharpnackRS:12, WangSST:15}. For example, if
$e_i$ is a directed edge that connects the $j$th node to the $k$th
node ($j < k$), the elements of the $i$th row of $\Delta$ are
\begin{equation*} \Delta_{i, \ell} = 
  \left\{ 
    \begin{array}{rl}
      - {\rm sgn}(\mathrm{W}_{j,k}) \sqrt{ | \mathrm{W}_{j,k} | }, & \ell = j;\\
       {\rm sgn}(\mathrm{W}_{j,k}) \sqrt{ | \mathrm{W}_{j,k} | }, & \ell = k;\\
      0, & \mbox{otherwise},
  \end{array} \right.
\end{equation*}
where $\mathrm{W}$ is the weighted adjacency matrix, sgn$(\cdot)$ denotes the sign, which is used to handle the negative edge weights.
nodes.origin_citation: Sharpnack, Rinaldo, Singh 2012; Wang, Sharpnack, Smola, Tibshirani 2015
nodes.statement_short: Edge-by-node oriented incidence matrix with entries -/+ sgn(W_jk) sqrt|W_jk| at the edge's endpoints.

nodes.name: Difference operator and Laplacian quadratic form
nodes.statement: When $G$ is an undirected graph, $\left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 = \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x}$, where $\mathrm{L}$ is the graph Laplacian matrix, which measures the total Lipschiz smoothness as shown in Definition~\ref{df:global_Lip}.
conclusions: $\left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 = \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x}$

nodes.name: Piecewise-constant graph signal with $K$ cuts
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N$ is~\emph{piecewise-constant} with $K \in \{0, 1, \cdots, N-1\}$ cuts, when it satisfies \begin{displaymath} \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \leq K. \end{displaymath}
nodes.label: df:pc_des

nodes.name: Inconsistent edge
nodes.statement: Each element of $\Delta \mathbf{x}$ is the difference between two adjacenct signal coefficient; when $\left( \Delta \mathbf{x} \right)_i \neq 0$, we call the $i$th edge is inconsistent.

nodes.name: Class $\mathrm{PC}_{G}(K)$
nodes.statement: The class $\mathrm{PC}_{G}(K)$ represents signals that contain at most $K$ inconsistent edges.

nodes.name: Local sets
nodes.statement: Let $\{S_c\}_{c=1}^C$ be the partition of the node set $\mathcal{V}$. We call $\{S_c\}_{c=1}^C$~\emph{local sets} when they satisfy that the subgraph corresponding to each local set is connected, that is, when $G_{S_c}$ is connected for all $c$.
nodes.genus: the partition of the node set $\mathcal{V}$
nodes.label: df:localset

nodes.name: Local-set-based graph signal
Normalized variation of a local set
nodes.statement:
For a local-set-based graph signal, we measure its smoothness by the normalized variation
$$
\mathrm{S}_{\Delta, p} (S) = \frac{1}{\left\|  {\bf 1}_S  \right\|_p^p}\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_S \right\|_p^p.
$$

nodes.name: Piecewise-constant graph signal based on local sets
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ is piecewise-constant based on local sets $\{S_c\}_{c=1}^C$ when \begin{equation*} \mathbf{x} \ = \ \sum_{c=1}^C a_c {\bf 1}_{S_c}, \end{equation*} where $\{S_c\}_{c=1}^C$ forms a valid series of local sets. Denote this class by $\mathrm{PC}(C)$.
nodes.label: df:pc_gen

nodes.name: Connection between generative and descriptive piecewise-constant models
nodes.statement: When the value of the graph signal on each local set is different, $\left\| \Delta \mathbf{x}  \right\|_0$ counts the total number of edges connecting nodes between local sets.
assumptions: When the value of the graph signal on each local set is different
conclusions: $\left\| \Delta \mathbf{x}  \right\|_0$ counts the total number of edges connecting nodes between local sets

nodes.name: General multiresolution analysis on graphs
nodes.statement: A general multiresolution analysis on graphs consists of a sequence of embedded closed subspaces \begin{equation*} V_0 \subset V_{1} \subset V_{2} \cdots \subset V_{K} \end{equation*} such that \begin{itemize} \item upward completeness \begin{equation*} \bigcup_{i=0}^K V_{i} = \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N; \end{equation*} \item downward completeness \begin{equation*} \bigcap_{i=0}^K V_{i} = \{ c {\bf 1_{\mathcal{V}}}, c \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} \}; \end{equation*} \item existence of basis \ There exists an orthonormal basis $\{\Phi\}_{i}$ for $V_K$. \end{itemize}
nodes.genus: a sequence of embedded closed subspaces
nodes.statement_short: Nested subspaces V_0 in ... in V_K whose union is R^N, whose intersection is the constants, with an orthonormal basis of V_K.
nodes.label: df:MRA

nodes.name: Multiresolution local set construction
nodes.statement:
We initialize $S_{0,1} = \mathcal{V}$
to correspond to the $0$th level subspace $V_0$, that is, $V_0 = \{
c_0 {\bf 1}_{S_{0,1}}, c_0 \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} \}$. We then partition $S_{0,1}$
into two disjoint local sets $S_{1,1}$ and $S_{1,2}$, corresponding to the first level subspace $V_1$, where $V_1 = \{ c_1 {\bf 1}_{S_{1,1}}
+ c_2 {\bf 1}_{S_{1,2}}, c_1, c_2 \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} \}$. We then
recursively partition each larger local set into two smaller local
sets. For the $i$th level subspace, we have $V_i = \sum_{j=1}^{2^i}
c_j {\bf 1}_{S_{i,j}}$ and then, we partition $S_{i,j}$ into
$S_{i+1,2j-1}, S_{i+1,2j}$ for all $j = 1, 2, \ldots, 2^i$.  We call
$S_{i,j}$ the parent set of $S_{i+1,2j-1}, S_{i+1,2j}$ and
$S_{i+1,2j-1}, S_{i+1,2j}$ are the children sets of $S_{i,j}$. When
$|S_{i,j}| \leq 1$, $S_{i+1,2j-1} = S_{i,j}$ and $S_{i+1,2j} =
\emptyset$. At the finest resolution, each local set corresponds to an
individual node or an empty set.
nodes.statement_short: Recursively bisect each local set into two connected local sets, level by level, until every set is a single node; level i spans V_i.

nodes.name: Local set decomposition tree
nodes.statement:
In other words, we build a binary
decomposition tree that partitions a graph structure into multiple
local sets. The $i$th level of the decomposition tree corresponds to
the $i$th level subspace.

nodes.name: Depth $T$ of the decomposition
nodes.statement:
The depth of the decomposition $T$
depends on how local sets are partitioned; $T$ ranges from
$N$ to $\ceil*{\log N}$, where $N$ corresponds to partitioning one
node at a time and $\ceil*{\log N}$ corresponds to an even partition
at each level.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6 (construction satisfies MRA)
nodes.statement:
It is clear that the proposed construction of local sets satisfies three requirements in Definition~\ref{df:MRA}. The initial subspace $V_0$ has the coast resolution. Through partitioning, local sets zoom into
increasingly finer resolutions in the graph vertex domain. The subspace $V_T$ with finest resolution zoom into each individual node and covers the entire $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N$.  Classical scale invariance requires that when $f(t) \in V_0$, then $f(2^m t) \in V_m$, which is ill-posed
in the graph domain because graphs are finite and discrete;
the classical translation invariance requires that when $f(t) \in
V_0$, then $f(t-n) \in V_0$, which is again ill-posed, this time
because graphs are irregular. The essence of scaling and translation
invariance, however, is to use the same function and its scales and
translates to span different subspaces, which is what the proposed
construction promotes. The scaling function is ${\bf 1}_{S}$; the hierarchy of partition is similar to the scaling and translation, that is, when ${\bf 1}_{S_{i,j}} \in \mathcal{V}_{i}$, then ${\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j-1}}, {\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j}} \in \mathcal{V}_{i+1}$, and when ${\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j-1}} \in \mathcal{V}_{i+1}$ then ${\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j}} \in \mathcal{V}_{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Check upward and downward completeness and the basis requirement directly from the recursive partition; scaling/translation are replaced by the indicator hierarchy.

nodes.name: Toy local set decomposition on four nodes
nodes.statement: We now show a toy example in Figure~\ref{fig:decomposition}. In Partition 1, we partition the entire node set $S_{0,1} = \mathcal{V} = \{1, 2, 3, 4 \}$ into two disjoint local sets $S_{1,1} =  \{1, 2 \}, S_{1,2} =  \{3, 4 \}$. Thus, $V_1 = \{ c_1  {\bf 1_{S_{1,1}}} +  c_2  {\bf 1_{S_{1,2}}}  , c_1, c_2 \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} \}$. Similarly, in Partition 2, we partition $S_{1,1}$ into two disjoint connected sets $S_{2,1} =  \{1 \}, S_{2,2}  =  \{ 2 \}$; in Partition 3, we partition $S_{1,2}$ into $S_{2,3}  =  \{3 \}, S_{2,4}  =  \{ 4 \}$. Thus, $V_2 = \{ c_1  {\bf 1_{S_{2,1}}} +  c_2  {\bf 1_{S_{2,2}}} + c_3 {\bf 1_{S_{2,3}}} +  c_4  {\bf 1_{S_{2,4}}} , c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4 \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} \} = \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^4$.
nodes.statement_short: Partition {1,2,3,4} into {1,2},{3,4}, then into singletons; V_2 = R^4.

nodes.name: Graph partition problem for local sets
nodes.statement:
From the perspective of promoting smoothness of graph signals, we partition a local set $S$ into two disjoint local set $S_1, S_2$ by solving the following optimization problem
\begin{eqnarray} & \min_{S_1, S_2} & \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_1) + \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_2)
\\
\nonumber
& {\rm subject~to:} & S_1 \cap S_2 = \emptyset, S_1 \cup S_2 = S, 
\\
\nonumber
&& G_{S_1}~{\rm and}~G_{S_2}  {\rm~are~connected}.
\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Split a local set into two connected local sets minimizing the sum of their normalized variations.

nodes.name: Graph partition optimization (7)
nodes.statement: & \min_{S_1, S_2} & \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_1) + \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_2) \\ \nonumber & {\rm subject~to:} & S_1 \cap S_2 = \emptyset, S_1 \cup S_2 = S, \\ \nonumber && G_{S_1}~{\rm and}~G_{S_2} {\rm~are~connected}.
nodes.label: algo:partition

nodes.name: Spectral clustering partition
nodes.statement: The first one is based on spectral clustering~\cite{Luxburg:07}. We first obtain the graph Laplacian matrix of a local set and compute the eigenvector corresponding to the second smallest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian matrix. We then set the median number of the eigenvector as the threshold; we put the nodes whose corresponding values in the eigenvector are no smaller than the threshold into a children local set and put the nodes whose corresponding values in the eigenvector are smaller than the threshold into the other children local set. This method approximately solves~\ref{algo:partition} by ignoring the second constraint; it guarantees that two children local sets have the same number of nodes, but does not guarantee that they have the same number of nodes are connected.
nodes.statement_short: Threshold the Fiedler vector of the local set's Laplacian at its median to split it into two equal halves.

nodes.name: Spanning tree partition
nodes.statement: The second one is based on spanning tree. To partition a local set, we first obtain the maximum spanning tree of the subgraph and then find a balance node in the spanning tree. The balance node partition the spanning tree into two subtrees with the closet number of nodes~\cite{SharpnackKS:13}. We remove the balance node from the spanning tree, the resulting largest connected component form a children local set and the other nodes including the balance node forms the other children local set. This method approximately solves~\ref{algo:partition} by approximating a subgraph by the corresponding maximum spanning tree; it guarantee that two children local sets are connected, but does not guarantees that they have the same number of nodes. When the original sbugraph is highly connected, the spanning tree loses some connection information and the shape of the local set may not capture the community in the subgraph.
nodes.statement_short: Remove a balance node of the maximum spanning tree; the largest remaining component is one child local set.

nodes.name: 2-means partition
nodes.statement: The third one is based on the 2-means clustering. We first randomly select 2 nodes as the community center and assign every other node to its nearest community center based on the geodesic distance. We then recompute the community center for each community by minimizing the summation of the geodesic distances to all the other nodes in the community and assign node to its nearest community center again. We keep doing this until the community centres converge after a few iterations. This method is inspired from the classical $k$-means clustering; it also guarantees that two children local sets are connected, but does not guarantees that they have the same number of nodes.
nodes.statement_short: 2-means clustering with geodesic distances: assign nodes to the nearer of two centers, recompute centers, iterate to convergence.

nodes.name: Local-set-based piecewise-constant dictionary
nodes.statement:
We collect local sets by level in
ascending order in a dictionary, with atoms corresponding to each
local set, that is, $ \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC} = \{ {\bf 1}_{S_{i, j}} \}_{i=0, j = 1}^{i=T, j = 2^i}$.
We call it the~\emph{local-set-based piecewise-constant dictionary}.
nodes.statement_short: D_LSPC: indicator atoms of all multiresolution local sets.

nodes.name: Local-set-based wavelet basis
nodes.statement:
We combine two local sets partitioned from the same parent local set to form a basis vector. Let the local sets $S_{i+1,2j-1}, S_{i+1,2j}$ have the same parent local set $S_{i,j}$, the basis vector combing these two local sets is
\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \sqrt{ \frac{|S_{i+1,2j-1}| |S_{i+1,2j}|}{|S_{i+1,2j-1}|+|S_{i+1,2j}|}} \bigg(  \frac{1}{|S_{i+1,2j-1}|} {\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j-1}} 
\\
&& - \frac{1}{|S_{i+1,2j}|} {\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j}} \bigg).
\end{eqnarray*}
To represent in a matrix form, the wavelet basis is
\begin{eqnarray*}
\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC} = \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC} \mathrm{D}_2,
\end{eqnarray*}
where the downsampling matrix
\begin{eqnarray*}
 \mathrm{D}_2 & = &
 \begin{bmatrix}
 \frac{1}{\left\| \mathbf{d}_1 \right\|_2} & \phantom{+}0  & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
 0 & \phantom{+} g(\mathbf{d}_2, \mathbf{d}_3)  & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
 0 & -g(\mathbf{d}_3, \mathbf{d}_2)  & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
  0 & \phantom{+}0 & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
 0 & \phantom{+}0   & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
 \vdots & \phantom{+}\vdots & \ddots & \phantom{+}\vdots \\
  0 & \phantom{+}0  & \cdots & \phantom{+}g(\mathbf{d}_{2N-2}, \mathbf{d}_{2N-1} )  \\
 0 & \phantom{+}0  & \cdots & -g(\mathbf{d}_{2N-1}, \mathbf{d}_{2N-2}) \\
 \end{bmatrix}
 \\
 & \in  & \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{(2N-1) \times N},
\end{eqnarray*}
with $\mathbf{d}_i$ is the $i$th column of $\mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC}$, and 
 $$
 g(\mathbf{d}_i, \mathbf{d}_j) = \sqrt{ \frac{\left\| \mathbf{d}_j \right\|_0} { ( \left\| \mathbf{d}_i \right\|_0  + \left\| \mathbf{d}_j \right\|_0 ) \left\| \mathbf{d}_i \right\|_0  }}.
 $$
The downsampling matrix $\mathrm{U}_2$ combines two consecutive column vectors in $\mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC}$ to form one column vector in $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$ and the function $g(\cdot, \cdot)$ reweights the column vectors in $\mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC}$ to ensure that each column vector in $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$ has norm 1 and sums to 0.
nodes.statement_short: Each split of a parent set into two children yields a normalized Haar-like vector; W_LSPC = D_LSPC D_2.

nodes.name: Wavelet basis vectors of the toy decomposition
nodes.statement_short: The three partitions of {1,2,3,4} give the vectors (1,1,-1,-1)/2, (1,-1,0,0)/sqrt2, (0,0,1,-1)/sqrt2.

nodes.name: Local-set-based Wavelet Basis Construction
nodes.statement: \footnotesize \caption{ Local-set-based Wavelet Basis Construction } \begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}} \addlinespace[1mm] {\bf Input} & $G(\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E}, \mathrm{A} )$~~graph \\ {\bf Output} & $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$~~~~~~wavelet basis \\ \addlinespace[2mm] {\bf Function} & &\\ & initialize a stack of node sets $\mathbb{S}$ and a set of vectors $\mathrm{W}$ \\ & push $S = \mathcal{V}$ into $\mathbb{S}$ \\ & add $\mathbf{w} = \frac{1}{ \sqrt{|S|}} {\bf 1}_S$ into $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$ \\ & while the cardinality of the largest element of $\mathbb{S}$ is bigger than $1$ \\ &~pop up one element from $\mathbb{S}$ as $S$ \\ &~partition $S$ into two disjoint connected sets $S_1, S_2$ \\ &~push $S_1, S_2$ into $\mathbb{S}$ \\ &~add $\mathbf{w} = \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \left( \frac{1}{|S_1|} {\bf 1}_{S_1} - \frac{1}{|S_2|} {\bf 1}_{S_2}\right)$ into $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$\\ & end \\ & {\bf return} $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$ \\ \addlinespace[1mm] \end{tabular}
nodes.statement_short: Stack-based recursive bisection of the node set; each split adds a normalized Haar-like vector to W_LSPC.
nodes.label: alg:wavelet

nodes.name: Local set construction satisfies multiresolution analysis
nodes.statement: The proposed construction of local sets satisfies the multiresolution analysis on graphs.
conclusions: The proposed construction of local sets satisfies the multiresolution analysis on graphs.
nodes.label: thm:MRA

nodes.name: Finer local sets are less smooth
nodes.statement: A series of local sets with a finer resolution is less smooth, that is, for all $i$, \begin{equation*} \sum_{j=1}^{2^i} \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_{i,j}) \leq \sum_{j=1}^{2^{i+1}} \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_{i+1,j}) . \end{equation*}
conclusions: A series of local sets with a finer resolution is less smooth
nodes.statement_short: Total normalized variation of the local sets is nondecreasing with the decomposition level.
nodes.label: thm:smooth

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7
nodes.statement: We first show that the sum of variations of two children local sets is larger than the variation of the parent local set. \begin{eqnarray*} && \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_{i+1,2j-1}) + \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_{i+1,2j}) \\ & = & \frac{1}{ |S_{i+1,2j-1}| }\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j-1} } \right\|_0 + \frac{1}{ |S_{i+1,2j}| }\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j} } \right\|_0 \\ & \stackrel{(a)}{ \geq } & \frac{1}{ |S_{i,j}| } \left( \left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j-1} } \right\|_0 + \left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j} } \right\|_0 \right) \\ & \stackrel{(b)}{\geq} & \frac{1}{ |S_{i,j}| }\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{S_{i,j}} \right\|_0 \ = \ \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_{i,j}), \end{eqnarray*} where $(a)$ follows from that the cardinality of the the parent local set is larger than either of its children local sets and $(b)$ follows from that we need to cut a boundary to partition two children local sets. Since every local set in the $i$th level has two children local sets in the $i+1$th level and every local set in the $i+1$th level has a parent local set in the $i$th local, we sum them together and obtain Theorem~\ref{thm:smooth}.
nodes.statement_short: Show two children have larger summed variation than their parent (smaller sizes, extra cut), then sum over the level.

nodes.name: Local-set-based wavelet basis is orthonormal
nodes.statement: The local-set-based wavelet basis constructs an orthonormal basis.
conclusions: The local-set-based wavelet basis constructs an orthonormal basis.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8
nodes.statement: First, we show each vector has norm one. \begin{eqnarray*} && \left\| \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \left( \frac{1}{ | S_1 |} {\bf 1}_{S_1} - \frac{1}{| S_2 |} {\bf 1}_{S_2}\right) \right\|_2^2 \\ & \stackrel{(a)}{=} & |S_1| \left( \sqrt{\frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \frac{1}{ | S_1 |} \right)^2 + |S_2| \left( \sqrt{\frac{|S_1| |S_1|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \frac{1}{ | S_2 |} \right)^2 \\ & = & 1, \end{eqnarray*} where $(a)$ follows from that $S_1 \cap S_2 = \emptyset$. Second, we show each vector is orthogonal to the other vectors. We have \begin{eqnarray*} {\bf 1}^T \mathbf{w} = \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \left( \sum_{i \in S_1} \frac{1}{ | S_1 |} - \sum_{i \in S_2} \frac{1}{| S_2 |} \right) = 0. \end{eqnarray*} Thus, each vector is orthogonal to the first vector, ${\bf 1}_{\mathcal{V}}/\sqrt{|{\mathcal{V}}| }$. Each other individual vector is generated from two node sets. Let $S_1, S_2$ generate $\mathbf{w}_i$ and $S_3, S_4$ generate $\mathbf{w}_j$. Due to the construction, there are only two conditions, two node sets of one vector belongs to one node set of the other vector, and all four node sets do not share element with each other. For the first case, without losing generality, let $\left( S_3 \cup S_4 \right) \cap S_1= S_3 \cup S_4$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} \mathbf{w}_i^T \mathbf{w}_j & = & \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|} \frac{|S_3| |S_4|}{|S_3|+|S_4|}} \left( \sum_{i \in S_3} \frac{1}{ | S_3 |} - \sum_{i \in S_4} \frac{1}{| S_4 |} \right) \\ & = & 0. \end{eqnarray*} For the second case, the inner product between $\mathbf{w}_i$ and $\mathbf{w}_j $ is zero because their supports do not match. Third, we show that $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$ spans $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N$. Since we recursively partition the node set until the cardinalities of all the node sets are smaller than 2, there are $N$ vectors in $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$.
nodes.statement_short: Check unit norm, orthogonality (nested or disjoint supports) and that there are N vectors.

nodes.name: Sparsity of local-set-based wavelet coefficients
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{W}$ be the output of Algorithm~\ref{alg:wavelet} and $T$ be the maximum level of the decomposition in Algorithm~\ref{alg:wavelet} . For all $\mathbf{x} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} \left\| \mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}^T \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \leq \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 T. \end{eqnarray*}
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{W}$ be the output of Algorithm~\ref{alg:wavelet} and $T$ be the maximum level of the decomposition in Algorithm~\ref{alg:wavelet} .
conclusions: \left\| \mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}^T \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \leq \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 T.
nodes.statement_short: The number of nonzero wavelet coefficients is at most the number of inconsistent edges times the depth T.
nodes.label: thm:sparse

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9
nodes.statement: When an edge $e \in {\rm Supp}(\Delta \mathbf{w})$, where Supp denotes the indices of nonzero elements, we call that the edge $\mathbf{e}$ is activated by the vector $\mathbf{w}$. Since each edge is activated at most once in each decomposition level, so each edge is activated by at most $T$ basis elements. Let activations($e$) be the number of basis elements in $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$ that activates $e$. \begin{eqnarray*} \left\| \mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}^T \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \leq \sum_{ e \in {\rm Supp}(\Delta \mathbf{w}) } {\rm activations}(e) \leq \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 T. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Counting argument: each inconsistent edge activates at most one basis vector per decomposition level.

nodes.name: Even partition gives the Haar wavelet basis
nodes.statement: Note that when the partition is perfectly even, the resulting wavelet basis is the same with the classical Haar wavelet basis.
assumptions: when the partition is perfectly even
conclusions: the resulting wavelet basis is the same with the classical Haar wavelet basis

nodes.name: Sparse coding with the local-set-based piecewise-constant dictionary
nodes.statement: For all $\mathbf{x} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N$, we have $\left\| \mathbf{a}^* \right\|_0 \leq 2 T \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0$, where $T$ is the maximum level of the decomposition and \begin{eqnarray*} \mathbf{a}^* & = & \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}} \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0, \\ && {\rm subject~to:~} \mathbf{x} \ = \ \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC} \mathbf{a}. \end{eqnarray*}
conclusions: $\left\| \mathbf{a}^* \right\|_0 \leq 2 T \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0$
nodes.statement_short: The sparsest exact D_LSPC representation uses at most 2T||Delta x||_0 atoms.
nodes.label: thm:sparse

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{W}$ is obtained from $ \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC}$,  the worst case is to represent $\mathbf{x}$ by using $\mathrm{W}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each wavelet vector combines two dictionary atoms, so the wavelet expansion bounds the sparsest dictionary representation.

nodes.name: Sparsity of wavelet coefficients under even partition
nodes.statement: Let the local-set-based wavelet basis evenly partition the node set each time. We have \begin{eqnarray*} \left\| \mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}^T \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \leq \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \ceil*{\log N}. \end{eqnarray*}
assumptions: Let the local-set-based wavelet basis evenly partition the node set each time.
conclusions: \left\| \mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}^T \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \leq \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \ceil*{\log N}.

nodes.name: Optimality of the even-partition local-set wavelet basis
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{W}$ be the local-set-based wavelet basis with the even partition. Then, \begin{eqnarray*} \mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC} & = & \arg \min_{\mathrm{F}} \max_{\mathbf{x} \in \{ \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \leq K \} } \left\| \mathrm{F}^T \mathbf{x} \right\|_0, \\ && {\rm subject~to}: \mathrm{F} {\rm~is~orthornormal}. \end{eqnarray*}
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{W}$ be the local-set-based wavelet basis with the even partition.
conclusions: \mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC} & = & \arg \min_{\mathrm{F}} \max_{\mathbf{x} \in \{ \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_0 \leq K \} } \left\| \mathrm{F}^T \mathbf{x} \right\|_0,
nodes.statement_short: The even-partition wavelet basis minimizes the worst-case sparsity over orthonormal bases for signals with at most K inconsistent edges.

nodes.name: Difference operator versus local-set wavelet basis
nodes.statement: In general, the graph difference operator provides more sparse representation than the local-set-based wavelet basis, however, the graph difference operator is not necessarily a one-to-one mapping and is bad at reconstruction; the graph difference operator only focuses on the pairwise relationship. On the other hand, the local-set-based wavelet basis is good at reconstruction and provides multiresolution view in the graph vertex domain.

nodes.name: Even partition is not always best
nodes.statement: The even partition minimizes the worst case; it does not necessarily mean that the even partition is good for all the applications. For example, a graph has two communities, a huge one and a tiny one, which hints that a piecewise-constant graph signal sits on a part of either of two communities. In this case, we cut a few edges to partition two communities and assign a local set for each of them, instead of partitioning the huge community to make sure that two local sets have a same cardinality.

nodes.name: Sparse coding with a redundant dictionary
nodes.statement:
Since the the windowed graph dictionary and the local-set-based piecewise-constant dictionaries are redundant, we solve the following sparse coding problem,
\begin{eqnarray} \mathbf{x}' =  &  \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}} & \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{D} \mathbf{a}  \right\|_2^2,
   \\
   \nonumber
   & {\rm subject~to:~} &  \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K,
\end{eqnarray}
where $\mathrm{D}$ is a redundant dictionary and $\mathbf{a}$ is a sparse code.

nodes.name: Sparse coding problem (9)
nodes.statement: \mathbf{x}' = & \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}} & \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{D} \mathbf{a} \right\|_2^2, \\ \nonumber & {\rm subject~to:~} & \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K,
nodes.label: eq:sparse_coding_pc

nodes.name: Piecewise-constant signal on the U.S. city graph
nodes.statement:
Based on the  geographical area, we partition the nodes into four communities, including the north area (N), the middle area (M), the south area (S), and the west area (W). The corresponding piecewise-constant graph signal is
\begin{equation} \mathbf{x} =  {\bf 1}_{N} + 2 \cdot {\bf 1}_{M} + 3 \cdot {\bf 1}_{S} + 4 \cdot {\bf 1}_{W}.
\end{equation}
The graph signal is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:us_signal}(a), where dark blue indicates the north area, the light  indicates the middle area, the dark yellow indicates the south area and  the light yellow indicates the west area. The signal contains $4$ piecewise constants and $144$ inconsistent edges.
nodes.statement_short: Four geographic communities with values 1-4 give a piecewise-constant signal with 144 inconsistent edges.

nodes.name: U.S. piecewise-constant signal (10)
nodes.statement: \mathbf{x} = {\bf 1}_{N} + 2 \cdot {\bf 1}_{M} + 3 \cdot {\bf 1}_{S} + 4 \cdot {\bf 1}_{W}.
nodes.label: eq:pc_us

nodes.name: Local-set representations approximate piecewise-constant signals well
nodes.statement: To summarize the task of approximation, the proposed local set based representations provide a reliable approximation to a piecewise-constant graph signal because of the sparsity promotion.
conclusions: the proposed local set based representations provide a reliable approximation to a piecewise-constant graph signal

nodes.name: Local-set-based recovery algorithm (center-assign)
nodes.statement_short: Partition into M leaf local sets (largest first), sample each set's geodesic center, and assign its value to the whole set.
input: Let $m$ be the number of samples.

nodes.name: Recovery error bound for the local-set-based recovery algorithm
nodes.statement: Let the original graph signal $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{PC}_G(K)$. The recovery error is bounded as \begin{eqnarray*} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathrm{I} ( x_i \neq x'_i ) \leq K \max_{j = 1, \cdots, M} | S_j |, \end{eqnarray*} where $\mathrm{I} (\cdot)$ is the indicator function.
conclusions: \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathrm{I} ( x_i \neq x'_i ) \leq K \max_{j = 1, \cdots, M} | S_j |,
nodes.statement_short: The number of mislabeled nodes is at most K times the size of the largest leaf local set.
nodes.label: thm:recovery_err

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 10
nodes.statement: The error happens only when there exists at least one inconsistent edge in a community. Since there are $K$ inconsistent edges, we make errors in at most $K$ communities. The worst case is that each error is made in the one of the largest $K$ communities.
nodes.statement_short: Errors only occur in local sets containing an inconsistent edge; at most K such sets, worst case the K largest.

nodes.name: Even partition and experimentally designed sampling minimize the bound
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:recovery_err} shows that the size of the largest community influences the recovery error.  When we use the even partition, the size of the largest local set is minimized, which minimizes the upper bound. Similar to Theorem~\ref{thm:sparse}, Theorem~\ref{thm:recovery_err} also shows the importance of the even partition again. This algorithm studies the graph structure before taking samples, which belongs to the experimentally designed sampling. In the classical regression for piecewise-constant functions, it is known that experimentally designed sampling has the same performance with random sampling asymptotically~\cite{CastroWN:05}. When we restrict the problem setting to sample only a few nodes from a finite graph, however, random sampling can lead to the uneven partition where some communities are much larger than the others. As a deterministic approach, the experimentally designed sampling minimizes the error bound and is better than random sampling when the sample size is small.

nodes.name: Trend filtering on graphs (recovery)
nodes.statement:
For trend filtering on graphs, we consider
\begin{eqnarray*} \mathbf{x}' =  &  \arg \min_{\mathbf{t}} & \left\| \mathbf{x}_\mathcal{M} - \mathbf{t}_\mathcal{M}  \right\|_2^2 + \mu \left\| \Delta \mathbf{t} \right\|_1,
\end{eqnarray*}
where $\mathcal{M}$ is the sampling node set obtained by random sampling.
nodes.origin_citation: Wang, Sharpnack, Smola, Tibshirani 2015 (trend filtering on graphs)
nodes.statement_short: Recover by l2 fit at sampled nodes plus an l1 penalty on the graph differences.

nodes.name: Harmonic functions (recovery)
nodes.statement:
For harmonic functions, we consider
\begin{eqnarray*} \mathbf{x}' =  &  \arg \min_{\mathbf{t}} & \left\| \mathbf{x}_\mathcal{M} - \mathbf{t}_\mathcal{M}  \right\|_2^2 + \mu \left\| \Delta \mathbf{t} \right\|_2^2,
\end{eqnarray*}
where $\left\| \Delta \mathbf{t} \right\|_2^2 = \mathbf{t}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{t}$ and $\mathrm{L}$ is the graph Laplacian matrix. Harmonic functions are proposed to recover a smooth graph signal which can be treated as an approximation of a piecewise-constant graph signal. When we obtain the solution, we assign each coefficient to its closest constant in $\mathbf{x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recover by l2 fit at sampled nodes plus Laplacian smoothness, then round each value to the nearest constant.

nodes.name: Local-set-based recovery beats harmonic functions and trend filtering
nodes.statement: We see that the local-set-based recovery algorithms are better than harmonic functions and trend filtering, especially when the sample ratio is small.
conclusions: the local-set-based recovery algorithms are better than harmonic functions and trend filtering

nodes.name: Piecewise-polynomial graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ is piecewise-polynomial with $C$ pieces and degree $K$ when \begin{equation*} \mathbf{x} \ = \ \sum_{c=1}^C \mathbf{x}^{(c)} {\bf 1}_{ S_c}, \end{equation*} where $\mathbf{x}^{(c)}$ is a $k$th order polynomial signal on the subgraph $G_{S_c}$ with $x^{(c)}_i \ = \ a_{c} + \sum_{j \in S_c} \sum_{k=1}^K a_{k, j, c} d^k(v_i, v_j). $ Denote this class by $\mathrm{PPL}(C, K)$.
nodes.statement_short: Signals that are a degree-K graph polynomial on each of C local sets.

nodes.name: PPL generalizes polynomial and piecewise-constant classes
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{PPL}(1, K)$ is the polynomial class with degree $K$, $\mathrm{PL}(K)$ from Definition~\ref{df:polynomial_sig}, and $\mathrm{PPL}(C, 0)$ is the piecewise-constant class with $C$ pieces, $\mathrm{PC}(C)$ from Definition~\ref{df:pc_gen}.
conclusions: $\mathrm{PPL}(1, K)$ is the polynomial class with degree $K$, $\mathrm{PL}(K)$ from Definition~\ref{df:polynomial_sig}

nodes.name: Piecewise-bandlimited graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ is piecewise-bandlimited with $C$ pieces and bandwidth $K$ when \begin{equation*} \mathbf{x} \ = \ \sum_{c=1}^C \mathbf{x}^{(c)} {\bf 1}_{ S_c}, \end{equation*} where $\mathbf{x}^{(c)}$ is a bandlimited signal on the subgraph $G_{S_c}$ with $x^{(c)}_i = \sum_{k=0}^K a_{k, c} \mathrm{V}^{(c)}_{i,k}$, and $\mathrm{V}^{(c)}$ is a graph Fourier basis of $G_{S_c}$. Denote this class by $\mathrm{PBL}_{\mathrm{V}}(C, K)$.
nodes.statement_short: Signals that are K-bandlimited (in each piece's own graph Fourier basis) on each of C local sets.

nodes.name: Local polynomial sub-dictionary $\mathrm{D}_{S_{i,j}}$
Local-set-based piecewise-smooth dictionary
nodes.statement:
We collect the sub-dictionaries for all the multiresolution local sets to form the~\emph{local-set-based piecewise-smooth dictionary}, that is,
$ \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPS}~=~\{ \mathrm{D}_{S_{i, j}}  \}_{i=0, j = 1}^{T,  2^i} $.

nodes.name: Size of the local-set-based piecewise-smooth dictionary
nodes.statement: The number of atoms in $\mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPS}$ is $O(K N T)$, where $K$ is the maximum degree of polynomial, $N$ is the size of the graph and $T$ is the maximum level of the decomposition. When we use  even partitioning, the total number of atoms is $O(K N \log N)$.
conclusions: The number of atoms in $\mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPS}$ is $O(K N T)$

nodes.name: Sparse approximation of piecewise-bandlimited signals by D_LSPS
nodes.statement: For all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{PBL}_{\mathrm{V}_L}(C,K)$, where $\mathrm{V}_L$ is the graph Fourier basis of the graph Laplacian matrix $\mathrm{L}$, we have $\left\| \mathbf{a}^* \right\|_0 \leq 2 K T\left\| \Delta \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{PC}} \right\|_0$, where $T$ is the maximum level of the decomposition, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{PC}}$ is a piecewise-constant signal that corresponds the same local sets with $\mathbf{x}$ and \begin{eqnarray*} \mathbf{a}^* & = & \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}} \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0, \\ && {\rm subject~to~} \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPS} \mathbf{a} \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon_{\rm par} \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2, \end{eqnarray*} where $\epsilon_{\rm par} $ is a constant determined by graph partitioning.
assumptions: For all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{PBL}_{\mathrm{V}_L}(C,K)$, where $\mathrm{V}_L$ is the graph Fourier basis of the graph Laplacian matrix $\mathrm{L}$
conclusions: $\left\| \mathbf{a}^* \right\|_0 \leq 2 K T\left\| \Delta \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{PC}} \right\|_0$
nodes.statement_short: A piecewise-bandlimited signal is epsilon_par-approximated by at most 2KT||Delta x_PC||_0 atoms of D_LSPS.
nodes.label: thm:PPL

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: The main idea is that we approximate a bandlimited signal in the original graph by using bandlimited signals in subgraphs. Based on the eigenvectors of graph Laplacian matrix, we define the bandlimited space, where each signal can be represented as $\mathbf{x} = \mathrm{V}_{(K)} \mathbf{a},$ where $\mathrm{V}_{(K)}$ is the submatrix of $\mathrm{V}$ containing the first $K$ columns in $\mathrm{V}$. We can show that this bandlimited space is a subspace of the total pairwise smooth space $\{\mathbf{x}: \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x} \leq \lambda_K \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} \}$. \begin{eqnarray*} && \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x} \ = \ \sum_{i,j \in \mathcal{E}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} (x_i - x_j)^2 \\ & = & \sum_{S_c} \sum_{i,j \in \mathcal{E}_{S_c}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} (x_i - x_j)^2 + \sum_{i,j \in (\mathcal{E} / \cup_{c} \mathcal{E}_{S_c}) } \mathrm{W}_{i,j} (x_i - x_j)^2 \\ & = & \sum_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c} + \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x} \ \leq \ \lambda_K \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}, \end{eqnarray*} where $\mathrm{L}_{S_c}$ is the graph Laplacian matrix of the subgraph $G_{S_c}$ and $\mathrm{L}_{S_c}$ stores the residual edges, which are cut in the graph partition algorithm. Thus, $\{\mathbf{x}: \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x} \leq \lambda_K \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} \}$ is a subset of $\bigcup_{S_c} \{\mathbf{x}_{S_c}: \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c} \leq \lambda_K \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x} \}$; that is, any total pairwise smooth graph signal in the whole graph can be precisely represented by total pairwise smooth graph signals in the subgraphs. In each local set, when we use the bandlimited space $\{ \mathbf{x}: \mathbf{x} = {\mathrm{V}_{S_c}}_{(K)} \mathbf{a} \}$ to approximate the space $\{\mathbf{x}_{S_c}: \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c} \leq c \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathbf{x}_{S_c} \}$, the maximum error we suffer from is $c \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathbf{x}_{S_c} / \lambda^{(S_c)}_{K+1}$, which is solved by the following optimization problem, \begin{eqnarray*} && \max_{\mathbf{x}} \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{V}_{S_c} \mathrm{V}_{S_c}^T \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 \\ && {\rm subject~to:}~ \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x} \leq c \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}. \end{eqnarray*} In other words, in each local set, the maximum error to represent $ \{\mathbf{x}_{S_c}: \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c} \leq \lambda_K \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x} \}$ is $(\lambda_K \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x})/\lambda^{(S_c)}_{K+1}$. Since all the local sets share the variation budget of $\lambda_K \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}$ together, the maximum error we suffer from is $\epsilon_{\rm par} \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 = (\lambda_K \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x})/ \min_{S_c} \lambda^{(S_c)}_{K+1}$.
